title: Closeup of Region of Andromeda Galaxy and Star Clusters
caption: A region of the Andromeda Galaxy and its star clusters, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M31, Andromeda Galaxy · constellation Andromeda · about 2.5 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams, L.C. Johnson (University of Washington), and the PHAT team

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble close-up shows a region of the Andromeda galaxy, M31, along with some of its star clusters. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy and the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away in the constellation Andromeda.

The view comes from the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury, or PHAT, a survey of the galaxy's disk. Nearly 8,000 images of 117 million stars were taken in near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, and assembled into 414 mosaic photographs.

Using 2,753 young, blue star clusters found in those images, astronomers measured what share of a cluster's stars form at each mass. Andromeda and the Milky Way turned out to have a similar share of newborn stars by mass, and the distribution was very similar from cluster to cluster. The brightest, most massive stars were 25 percent less common than earlier research had predicted.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F336W in blue, F475W in green, F814W in yellow and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The image includes near-ultraviolet and near-infrared light, both invisible to the eye, and Hubble picks out individual stars in another galaxy.

explore: About 30,000 volunteers helped find the clusters through the Andromeda Project, hosted by Zooniverse. Over 25 days they made 1.82 million image classifications, raising the number of known clusters in the survey region by a factor of six. The clusters are between 4 million and 24 million years old.
